newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Finland Bank rejects EMU delay, sees Germany in.
newsitem.headline: Finland Bank rejects EMU delay, sees Germany in.

text.p: Bank of Finland central bank governor Sirkka Hamalainen was quoted by a Swiss newspaper as saying she was strictly against any delay in European single currency plans under Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
Hamalainen also told the Zurich daily Tages-Anzeiger she expected Germany and France to meet the Maastricht criteria for joing the Europan single curency club.
Asked what she thought of delaying the single currency, which is due to be launched on January 1, 1999, the governor said:
"I am strictly against this because it would unleash strong waves of speculation on financial markets," she said.
"In addition, I believe the same as the EU Commission that both Germany and France will fulfill the Maastricht criteria," she added in the interview, printed in German.
Hamalainen also said Finland would meet all the criteria and that she was confident parliament would approve the country's entry into the single currency.
"The only real opposition to Finland entering the currency union comes from the Centre Party and a few representatives of the left," she told the newspaper.
"I am certain that our parliament will approve of joining EMU. There are no plans for a referendum," Hamalainen said.
"Incidently, the unions are also in favour of a Euro membership," she added.

Hamalainen said she had nothing against French proposals for a "stability council" to coordinate economic policy alongside the new European Central Bank as long as its job was limited to coordination.
"But the independence of the Euro central bank must remain guaranteed," she said.
Hamalainen said Finland's export industry was competitive enough to continue in the new Euro currency environment, regardless of whether Nordic neighbours Sweden and Denmark join.
She said the Bank of Finland would not lose its freedom in EMU but instead would gain influence by having an equal voice with other member countries in the European Central Bank.
"Every country's vote has the same weight in the European Central Bank council. Anyway, we are not totally free to make our own decisions today, either," she said.
